strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated and technically coherent framework (InFOM) that combines three ideas—flow-matching occupancy models, variational intention inference, and implicit generalized policy improvement—into a unified pre-training/fine-tuning pipeline for offline RL, with clear theoretical grounding (ELBO derivation, information bottleneck connection, and discussion of implicit GPI convergence properties in the appendix).

Extensive empirical evaluation across 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks spanning two different benchmark suites (ExORL and OGBench) with 8 diverse and reasonably strong baselines representing multiple methodological categories (offline RL, representation learning, model-based, contrastive occupancy models, and zero-shot RL via FB/HILP), using 8 random seeds for state tasks and 4 for image tasks, which lends credibility to the reported improvements.

Careful and honest comparison to the closest prior work (Farebrother et al. 2025's TD flows), with an ablation (FB+FOM) explicitly isolating the contribution of the proposed variational intention encoder versus prior representation mechanisms, and an ablation isolating the implicit GPI contribution versus naive GPI and one-step policy improvement — showing meaningful, non-trivial gains in both cases.

Thorough reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameter tables, domain-specific tuning documented, algorithm pseudocode for both pre-training and fine-tuning phases, and an open-source implementation link is mentioned.

Additional experiments beyond the main comparison (convergence speed analysis, extensive hyperparameter ablations in the appendix) strengthen the empirical case and provide useful insights into what drives performance and which hyperparameters are sensitive.
weaknesses: Some results are mixed or modest: on 2 of 8 (or by some framing 2-3 of 9) domains InFOM does not clearly outperform baselines (e.g., cheetah, some cube double / puzzle tasks remain near-zero success for all methods), and the paper's headline aggregate statistics (1.8x median return improvement, 36% success rate increase) could be more transparently contextualized against the raw per-task table given the high variance and occasional near-zero performance across all methods on harder tasks (e.g., cube double, puzzle 4x4).

The method introduces many hyperparameters (latent dimension d, KL coefficient λ, expectile µ, BC coefficient α, N, T) that require per-domain tuning (Table 3), which the appendix ablations (Fig. 7e, 7f) show substantially affect performance; this raises reproducibility/practicality concerns and suggests the method may be more brittle than the main results suggest, especially given that a fair amount of the specific tuning appears to have been done per-domain using a validation task from within the same domain.

The consistency assumption (Assumption 1, that consecutive transitions share the same intention) is a fairly strong simplifying assumption for reducing trajectories to pairwise transitions; while acknowledged as a limitation, its practical impact on intention quality/interpretability is not deeply analyzed empirically (e.g., no qualitative visualization or quantitative validation of what the inferred latent intentions actually capture).

The related work and baseline comparisons, while broad, do not include comparisons to more recent generative/diffusion-based occupancy or world-model baselines beyond the single closest prior work (TD flows), and some baseline implementations (e.g., FB, HILP, CRL+IS) are adapted/reimplemented rather than using original codebases directly, which could introduce implementation-specific confounds not fully addressed by using a shared codebase.

The writing has minor clarity issues (e.g., a garbled sentence in Related Work: 'it does not learn multiple skills during pre-training. in that we also learn...') and some notational inconsistencies in Algorithm 1 (e.g., line 7-9 use z where s should appear, appearing to be typos) that could confuse readers trying to reproduce the method exactly from the pseudocode.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem: combining long-horizon occupancy prediction with intention modeling for offline RL pre-training/fine-tuning, and provides a reasonably clear theoretical derivation (ELBO, information-bottleneck connection) for the proposed latent variable model.

Broad empirical evaluation across 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks from two different benchmark suites (ExORL, OGBench), with 8 baselines spanning multiple pre-training paradigms (behavioral cloning, representation learning, model-based, contrastive/successor-feature methods, skill discovery).

Detailed ablations isolating the two main components (variational intention encoder vs. HILP/FB-style representations; implicit GPI vs. standard GPI vs. one-step PI), plus a convergence-speed analysis.
Reasonably thorough appendix with reproducibility details: hyperparameter tables, per-domain tuning protocol, open-source implementation claim, and compute information.

Clear, explicit positioning relative to the closest prior work (Farebrother et al.'s TD flows), articulating the specific differences (latent intention encoder vs. finite representation set, expectile-based implicit GPI vs. explicit GPI).
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: the core technical pieces (TD/SARSA flow matching for occupancy measures, VAE-style latent intention encoding, expectile regression for implicit GPI) are each drawn essentially unchanged from prior work (Farebrother et al. 2025, Kostrikov et al. 2022, Kingma & Welling 2013, Barreto et al. 2017). The contribution is primarily a combination/engineering of existing components rather than a new algorithmic or theoretical insight.

Mixed and often weak empirical results undercut the headline claims: on many of the hardest tasks (cube double, puzzle 4x4, several scene tasks) absolute success rates remain very low (often <15-30%) for InFOM and essentially zero for all methods, making the practical significance of the reported '36% improvement' or '1.8x median return improvement' questionable as these are likely driven by a small subset of tasks/domains rather than broad, robust gains.

Standard deviations are frequently very large relative to the means (e.g., cube single task 3: 56.4 ± 36.9; cheetah walk: 254.8 ± 158.6), suggesting substantial run-to-run variance and weakening confidence that the reported improvements are statistically meaningful rather than noise.

Heavy, domain-specific hyperparameter tuning is required (latent dimension d, KL coefficient λ, expectile µ, BC coefficient α each tuned per domain via extensive sweeps), which directly contradicts the paper's framing as a step toward foundation-model-style pre-training that should transfer with minimal task-specific tuning; the hyperparameter ablation (Fig. 7) shows large sensitivity to λ and α in particular.

The intention inference mechanism conditions only on a single next transition (s', a'), which is a very local/myopic signal for inferring what should be a temporally extended notion of 'user intention'; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation but does not provide evidence that intentions are meaningfully recovered beyond downstream task performance (no direct intention-recovery or interpretability analysis).

Ablation studies for intention encoding and policy extraction strategies are conducted on only 2-4 tasks total, which is a very small subset of the full 40-task benchmark and limits confidence that the conclusions generalize across domains.

The theoretical justification for the implicit GPI procedure (Appendix B.2) relies on strong idealized assumptions (infinite samples, optimal flow occupancy models, expectile µ→1) that are not met in practice, so the practical connection between the stated theory and the actual finite-sample, finite-µ algorithm is weak.

Some related/competitive recent methods (e.g., more modern offline RL or world-model baselines) are not included, and the FB+FOM variant that is 'equivalent to prior work' is only evaluated in a narrow ablation rather than the full benchmark, making the central claim of outperforming the closest related work less thoroughly substantiated.

strengths: Proposes a well-motivated combination of flow-matching occupancy models with a variational latent-intention encoder, addressing a genuine gap (prior occupancy models largely ignore user/task heterogeneity in offline datasets).

Extensive empirical evaluation: 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks spanning ExORL and OGBench, compared against 8 diverse baselines representing different pre-training paradigms (BC, representation learning, model-based, contrastive/discriminative occupancy models, zero-shot RL with FB/HILP).

Careful ablations isolating the contribution of each component: intention encoder vs. FB/HILP representations (Sec 5.2), implicit GPI vs. naive GPI vs. one-step PI (Sec 5.3), and convergence-speed analysis (Sec 5.4), which help justify design choices individually rather than only as an aggregate system.

Solid theoretical grounding: ELBO derivation for the intention encoder, its connection to an information bottleneck objective, and discussion of convergence properties of the implicit GPI/expectile distillation approach.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameter tables, common settings shared across baselines and method, pseudocode for both pre-training and fine-tuning stages, and a stated commitment to open-source release.

Clear and honest positioning relative to the closest related work (Farebrother et al.'s TD flows), explicitly explaining the technical differences (latent intention encoder vs. finite discrete FB-based GPI) and empirically demonstrating the resulting benefits.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core building blocks (flow-matching TD occupancy models from Farebrother et al., VAE-style amortized intention inference, expectile-based implicit GPI from IQL) are all adapted from existing work, and the paper's contribution is largely in the specific combination and engineering rather than a fundamentally new idea.

Performance gains are uneven across domains/tasks: on several OGBench domains (e.g., cube double, puzzle 4x4, scene tasks 2-5) absolute success rates remain low (often <30%) even though InFOM outperforms baselines relatively, raising questions about practical utility on harder long-horizon tasks.

The method requires substantial per-domain hyperparameter tuning (latent dimension d, KL coefficient λ, BC coefficient α, expectile µ all vary by domain in Table 3), and the hyperparameter ablation (Appendix D) shows λ and α materially affect performance, suggesting limited out-of-the-box robustness/generalization as a 'foundation model' claim would imply.

The consistency assumption underlying intention inference (only consecutive transitions share the same intention) is quite weak and could fail to capture longer-horizon intentions/tasks; this is acknowledged only briefly as a limitation without empirical stress-testing of how sensitive results are to violations of this assumption.

Some baselines (FB, HILP, CRL+IS, TD InfoNCE+IS) are reimplemented by the authors rather than using official tuned pipelines end-to-end, which raises some fairness/tuning-parity concerns, especially since these are the most conceptually related competitors.

The most directly comparable prior method (Farebrother et al., TD flows with GPI) is only a workshop paper and is only compared against in a limited 4-task ablation (as 'FB+FOM') rather than being included as a full baseline across all 40 tasks in the main benchmark table.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks spanning ExORL and OGBench benchmarks, compared against 8 diverse baselines spanning multiple pre-training paradigms (BC, representation learning, model-based, contrastive occupancy, unsupervised skill discovery).
Clear theoretical grounding: the ELBO derivation for the intention encoder and its connection to an information bottleneck objective is rigorous and clearly presented in the appendix.

Thoughtful ablations isolating the contribution of each component: intention encoding vs. HILP/FB representations (Sec 5.2, App F.2), implicit GPI vs. standard finite-sample GPI or one-step PI (Sec 5.3), number of sampled future states, dataset size scaling, and extensive hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (App F.6-F.8).

The t-SNE visualization of inferred intentions aligning with ground-truth pick/place behavior is a compelling qualitative demonstration that the latent variable model is capturing meaningful structure, unlike FB or HILP baselines.

Strong and consistent gains on harder tasks (jaco with sparse reward, OGBench manipulation domains, and visual tasks), along with a real-world-grounded evaluation on the RT-1 dataset with SimplerEnv, which strengthens claims of practical relevance.
The paper is reasonably reproducible, providing full hyperparameter tables, algorithm pseudocode, and stating an open-source implementation.
weaknesses: The core technical machinery (SARSA/TD flow matching for occupancy models) is directly adopted from Farebrother et al. (2025), a workshop paper; the main novelty is restricted to the intention latent variable formulation and the implicit GPI expectile trick, making the overall contribution somewhat incremental relative to this closely related prior work.

Performance is inconsistent across domains: on cheetah and quadruped ExORL domains InFOM is roughly on par with or sometimes worse than simpler baselines (e.g., cheetah walk: InFOM 254.8±158.6 vs. ReBRAC 443.4±15.3), and variance is very high on several tasks, undermining confidence in the reported gains.

Absolute performance on some of the hardest OGBench domains (cube double, scene, puzzle 4x4) remains low in absolute terms even for InFOM (e.g., single-digit to double-digit success rates on several cube double and puzzle tasks), so while relative improvements over baselines are large, the tasks are still largely unsolved.

The method requires substantial domain-specific hyperparameter tuning (latent dimension d, KL coefficient λ, expectile μ, BC coefficient α all vary considerably across domains in Table 3), which raises concerns about practical usability and the claimed 'foundation model' framing, given that pre-trained models still need heavy re-tuning per downstream domain.

Computational overhead of the method (ODE solving via Euler method for N=16 future states at each Q estimation and during actor updates) is not clearly discussed or compared to baselines in terms of wall-clock or FLOPs cost.

The consistency assumption (Assumption 1) underlying intention inference is a fairly strong assumption about intention persisting across single transitions, and while justified conceptually in the appendix, it is not empirically stress-tested (e.g., under intention-switching mid-trajectory or noisier real-world settings) beyond the RT-1 experiment, which itself lacks a clean separation of pre-training/fine-tuning data.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks across two distinct benchmark suites (ExORL, OGBench), plus a real-robot (RT-1) evaluation, which is a substantial engineering effort.

Thorough ablation studies covering nearly every design choice (latent dimension, number of Euler steps, expectile, KL coefficient, BC coefficient, number of sampled future states, pre-training/fine-tuning dataset size), which aids understanding of what drives performance.

The derivation connecting the ELBO objective to an information-bottleneck interpretation (Appendix C.1) and the discussion of implicit GPI convergence properties (Appendix C.2) give some theoretical grounding to the method.
Good reproducibility effort: full pseudocode (Algorithms 1-2), detailed hyperparameter tables, and a stated intention to release code.

The qualitative intention visualizations (t-SNE plots) provide some intuitive evidence that the learned latent variable captures semantically meaningful structure (e.g., pick vs. place) better than compared representation baselines.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is incremental: it largely combines existing components (TD/SARSA flow matching from Farebrother et al. 2025, a standard VAE-style amortized intention encoder, and IQL-style expectile regression for implicit GPI) without a clearly novel algorithmic or theoretical insight beyond this combination.

The most directly comparable prior method (Farebrother et al. 2025's TD flows with GPI, here called FB+FOM) is explicitly stated to be 'equivalent' to a baseline, yet it is excluded from the main large-scale comparison (Table 4/Fig. 3) and only appears in a small 4-task ablation (Sec 5.2/Appendix F.2), making the headline comparisons against weaker baselines (IQL, ReBRAC, etc.) less convincing as evidence of the paper's central claimed contribution (intention-conditioning).

Results show very high variance across seeds on many tasks (e.g., cheetah walk: 254.8 ± 158.6 vs. ReBRAC 443.4 ± 15.3; cheetah walk backward similarly), and InFOM actually underperforms simpler baselines like ReBRAC on several ExORL locomotion tasks (cheetah, walker domains), undermining the generality of the 'matches or surpasses on 6/8 domains' claim.

The strong aggregate improvement numbers (1.8x median return, 36% success rate increase) appear to be driven largely by a few outlier settings (sparse-reward jaco tasks, and very low-success OGBench manipulation tasks like cube double/puzzle 4x4 where all methods, including InFOM, achieve under ~30% success), which can inflate relative-improvement statistics while absolute task performance remains weak and practically unconvincing.

Appendix F.4 shows that much of the large jaco improvement is attributable to reward sparsity rather than a fundamental modeling advantage, suggesting the headline results may not generalize beyond this specific reward structure.

Extensive per-domain hyperparameter tuning is required (latent dimension d, expectile µ, KL coefficient λ, BC coefficient α all vary substantially by domain in Table 3), which conflicts with the paper's framing as a step toward foundation-model-style pre-training that should transfer with minimal retuning.

No analysis of computational overhead (ODE solving for flow matching, N=16 sample Q estimation) relative to baselines, despite this likely being substantial, limiting practical assessment of the method's cost-benefit tradeoff.

The theoretical justification for implicit GPI (Appendix C.2) relies on idealized assumptions (infinite samples, optimal flow model, expectile → 1) that are not met in practice, and the gap between this ideal and the actual finite-sample, finite-expectile implementation is not empirically quantified.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated integration of variational intention inference with flow-matching occupancy models, addressing two under-explored aspects (long-horizon reasoning and multi-user intention heterogeneity) simultaneously for RL pre-training.

Strong theoretical grounding: the ELBO derivation is connected to an information bottleneck interpretation, and the implicit GPI procedure is justified both practically (avoiding backprop through the ODE solver) and with convergence intuition tied to expectile regression theory.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 36 state-based and 4 image-based tasks (ExORL and OGBench) against 8 diverse and well-chosen baselines spanning behavioral cloning, representation learning, model-based, contrastive, and successor-feature-based methods.

Thorough and insightful ablations: latent intention visualizations (t-SNE) showing clearer intention clustering than FB/HILP baselines, comparison of implicit GPI vs. naive GPI vs. one-step PI, dataset size scaling studies, and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses.
Additional real-world robustness check on the RT-1 dataset with SimplerEnv evaluation, showing the method generalizes beyond simulated benchmarks.
Good reproducibility: detailed algorithm boxes (pre-training/fine-tuning), full hyperparameter tables, consistent codebase across baselines, and stated open-source release.

Clear and honest positioning relative to the closest prior work (Farebrother et al., 2025 TD-flows with GPI), explicitly identifying differences (latent variable model vs. finite representations, implicit GPI vs. explicit maximization) and empirically validating these design choices.
weaknesses: Results are mixed across domains: InFOM underperforms or ties several baselines on the easier ExORL domains (cheetah, quadruped) and some OGBench tasks (e.g., cube double task 4/5, scene task 4/5) show near-zero performance for all methods, limiting the generality of the claimed improvements.

Several results exhibit high variance across seeds (e.g., cheetah walk, cube single task 3, cube double task 1), which the paper attributes to MC Q-estimation noise but does not fully resolve, slightly undercutting the reliability of reported gains.

The consistency assumption (Assumption 1), reducing trajectory-level intentions to consecutive transition pairs, is a notable simplification acknowledged as a limitation but not empirically stress-tested (e.g., under longer/more complex composite tasks where intention may shift more gradually).

The method has many interacting components (intention encoder, SARSA flow loss, reward predictor, expectile-based critic, BC-regularized actor), and while ablations are provided, disentangling their individual necessity versus their interaction effects could be more systematic.

Baseline comparisons rely on domain-specific hyperparameter tuning for both InFOM and baselines using a single representative task per domain, which may not fully capture per-task variability and could introduce some asymmetry in tuning effort.

Image-based experiments use only 4 tasks with 4 seeds each, which is a relatively small and low-power evaluation for judging visual generalization claims (e.g., 31% improvement claim rests on limited statistical support).
